findings.F1: The idea's give-back sits almost entirely in volatile markets: on the active bars, the mean unusual 24-hour move is +0.65 % (t 5.3, n 2923) in the top tercile of the coin's 20-day volatility, against +0.07 % (t 1.1, n 2827) and +0.06 % (t 0.8, n 2839) in the lower two. Ranked by 20-day volatility over 90-day volatility instead, the top tercile gives +0.63 % (t 6.1, n 2523) and the lower two +0.08 % and +0.11 %. So only the volatile cases exceed the 0.19 % cost of a trade, by about 3.3 times; the rest are below it.
findings.F2: Volatility is not an effect of its own: at the same 00:00 UTC bars, when the 24-hour move and the post-settlement hour agree (no signal), the top relative-volatility tercile earns +0.007 % (t 0.06, n 2176) and the top absolute-volatility tercile +0.08 % (t 0.6, n 2536). A volatile market belongs to the brief's theory, because crowding, and the funding paid for it, is largest after strong moves.
findings.F3: Inside the volatile tercile the effect stays graded by the size of the 24-hour reversal against 20-day volatility: by quintile it is −0.06 %, +0.42 %, +0.59 %, +0.59 % and +1.75 % (top quintile t 5.6, n 557). Both sides hold there (short +0.73 %, t 4.3; long +0.56 %, t 3.2).
findings.F4: The book is sized against where the effect lives: the vol-target sizing holds a mean allocation of 0.70 on low-volatility cases, 0.48 on middle ones and 0.31 on high-volatility cases. It turns over 0.44 of a coin's value per coin-day, about 4.2 bp a day in costs at 0.095 % per side. That cost is larger than the book's 2.2 bp mean daily return on days in a position, which fails its 5 bp rule.
findings.F5: The effect fades over time: active-case unusual moves are +0.87 % in 2018 and +0.55 % in 2019, then +0.30 % in 2023, −0.03 % in 2024 and −0.16 % in 2025. The book loses in 2022, 2024 and 2025 (−1.3, −7.2 and −5.6 bp a day) while holding rose. This drives the weak Calmar of 0.07 and the shortfall against holding (Sharpe −0.30 below holding's). Even in the volatile tercile, 2024 and 2025 are negative (−0.27 % and −0.22 %).
findings.F6: The move peaks at 24 hours (+0.25 %, t 4.7) against +0.12 % at 12 hours and +0.19 % at 48 hours; in the top two reversal quintiles it is +0.48 % (t 5.2) at 24 hours and +0.28 % at 48 hours. The 24-hour horizon is right, and a longer holding would not raise the move per case.

ideas.idea: The larger the coin's 24-hour return after the first hour following the 00:00 UTC settlement runs against that hour's move, the more its return over the following 24 hours runs back toward that hour's direction. This holds only while the coin's 20-day volatility is high against its 90-day volatility, and the give-back grows with that ratio.
ideas.consequence: A trader would take the second-day give-back only when the coin's recent volatility is raised against its longer-run level, and would stand aside in calm markets where the move does not cover the cost.
ideas.name: settlement fade in volatile regimes

ideas.idea: While the coin's 20-day volatility is high, the larger the coin's 24-hour return after the first post-00:00-settlement hour runs against that hour's move, measured in units of that 20-day volatility, the larger the percentage return over the following 24 hours back toward that hour's direction.
ideas.consequence: A trader would put most of the risk on the largest reversals in volatile markets, where one case's move is several times the cost of a trade, rather than spreading it evenly or shrinking it as volatility rises.
ideas.name: largest volatile settlement reversals
